title.en: Radioactivity, fission, fusion and nuclear energy
A forgotten drawer and a new science

text.en: In 1896 Henri Becquerel left uranium salts in a drawer on top of an unexposed photographic plate. When he developed the plate it was fogged, as if exposed to light. Uranium was giving out invisible rays by itself, and the science of radioactivity began.

In 1896 Henri Becquerel discovered radioactivity from uranium; the Curies later found it in pitchblende, an ore of uranium.
The spontaneous emission of alpha, beta and gamma radiations from certain elements is called radioactivity, and such elements are radioactive.
Natural radioactivity is spontaneous; elements with atomic number above 82, such as uranium and radium, show it, and only technetium (43) and promethium (61) below 82.
Alpha particles are helium nuclei with +2 charge, beta particles are fast electrons, and gamma rays are electromagnetic waves; gamma penetrates most and alpha least.
In alpha decay the atomic number falls by 2 and the mass number by 4; in beta decay the atomic number rises by 1 and the mass number is unchanged (Soddy and Fajan's displacement law).
Nuclear fission splits a heavy nucleus such as uranium-235 by a neutron into two lighter nuclei and releases huge energy with more neutrons, which can cause a chain reaction.
A controlled chain reaction runs a nuclear reactor, while an uncontrolled one gives an atom bomb; nuclear fusion joins light nuclei such as hydrogen into helium, as in the Sun and the hydrogen bomb.
Radioactivity is used in medicine, power generation, carbon dating and tracing, but radioactive material needs precautions such as lead shielding and dosimeters.

problem.en: Uranium-238 (atomic number 92) emits one alpha particle. What are the atomic number and mass number of the new nucleus?

text.en: Alpha decay reduces atomic number by 2: 92 - 2 = 90.

prompt.en: Compare alpha, beta and gamma rays and explain fission and fusion.

Fission splits heavy nuclei, fusion joins light nuclei
